message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 on consumer devices). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores. |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, etc., optimized for low latency. | Simpler, lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich, general‑purpose instruction sets (x86, ARM, etc.) with support for complex control flow. | Often a reduced instruction set tailored to SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers, and support for out‑of‑order execution. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies heavily on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory pools. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, I/O, OS services, single‑threaded applications. | Highly parallel tasks: image/video processing, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Latency vs throughput** | Low latency – quick response to individual instructions. | High throughput – many operations completed per cycle, but higher latency per operation. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional imperative programming, multithreading via OS threads or libraries like OpenMP. | SIMD/SIMT models (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute shaders), often requires explicit data parallelism. |

In short, CPUs excel at handling diverse, irregular workloads with low latency, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on many data elements in parallel, trading off per‑instruction complexity for massive throughput.
